Commonwealth
KOM-un-welth
n.
A compound of common and wealth (weal, well-being), from Old English commun and wela; appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Paul's description of the Gentiles' former standing before Christ.

Biblical Definition

Being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise.

Commonwealth appears once in the Authorized Version, in Paul's letter to the Ephesians, describing what Gentile believers had been before their union with Christ: aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world (Eph 2:12). The word names Israel's whole covenant polity — its citizenship, its promises, its access to God through the appointed means He had given — from which Gentiles by birth stood entirely excluded, outsiders to a national and spiritual body they had no natural claim upon. Paul's point is not to dwell on that former exclusion but to magnify the reversal Christ accomplished: but now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ (Eph 2:13), breaking down the middle wall of partition (Eph 2:14) so completely that Gentile believers are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints, and of the household of God (Eph 2:19). The passage stands as one of the New Testament's clearest statements that the church is not a replacement commonwealth built from scratch but the same covenant people of God now opened, in Christ, to Jew and Gentile alike, one new man, so making peace (Eph 2:15).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828), a compound of COMMON and WEALTH: the body politic; the whole community united under one polity; here of Israel's covenant citizenship from which Gentiles were formerly excluded.

COMMON, adj. Belonging equally to more than one; shared.

COMMONWEALTH, n. A body politic; a state; a community united for the common good.

In Ephesians 2:12 the word names Israel's covenant citizenship, from which Gentiles were once excluded.

Paul's larger point is the reversal Christ accomplished, breaking down 'the middle wall of partition' (Eph 2:14).

Gentile believers become 'fellow citizens with the saints, and of the household of God' (Eph 2:19).

Key Scripture

Eph 2:12 — "That at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world:"

Modern Corruption

A replacement-theology reading that treats the church as an entirely new entity severed from Israel's covenant history misses Paul's own language of Gentiles being grafted into, not replacing, the commonwealth and covenants Israel already possessed.

expand to see more

Some frameworks speak as though the church begins a wholly new story unconnected to Israel's covenants; Paul's own image is inclusion and access, not replacement — Gentiles made nigh, brought near to a commonwealth and covenants that already existed.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Paul's own: the dividing wall is broken down so that Jew and Gentile together form 'one new man' (Eph 2:15), united in the one commonwealth of God's people rather than two separate peoples merely coexisting.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Commonwealth occurs once, in Paul's description of the Gentiles' former exclusion from Israel's covenant polity, a standing entirely reversed in Christ, who breaks down the dividing wall and unites Jew and Gentile as one people of God.

Commonwealth in Ephesians 2:12 names Israel's covenant polity, from which Gentiles were formerly excluded.

The exclusion is paired with being 'strangers from the covenants of promise... without God in the world.'

Ephesians 2:13 announces the reversal: 'now in Christ Jesus ye... are made nigh by the blood of Christ.'

Ephesians 2:14 names Christ as the one who broke down 'the middle wall of partition.'

Ephesians 2:19 concludes: Gentile believers are 'fellow citizens with the saints, and of the household of God.'
